title: COP31: 7,500 cities outpace national governments in climate targets, says global alliance
content: Global Covenant of Mayors' report shows cities are leading climate action, with 58% of its signatories setting higher emissions targets than national governments. However, access to climate finance, especially in emerging markets, remains a critical challenge. The alliance plans to focus on implementation through enhanced urban climate finance and innovative solutions. More than half the cities and local governments participating in a global climate alliance have set emissions reduction targets that exceed their national governments' ambitions, and nearly one-third aim to achieve their targets sooner, according to a new report launched at the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) in Antalya, Türkiye.

title: COP31: UN chief calls for faster phase-out of fossil fuels and increased climate finance
content: At COP31, UN Secretary-General António Guterres has urged countries to phase out unabated use of coal by 2040, cut oil and gas use by a third and reduce global greenhouse gas emissions by 6 per cent annually. Guterres said current national climate plans deliver only about a third of the reductions required to keep the 1.5°C temperature goal within reach. Climate finance remains inadequate, with developing countries needing an estimated $305 billion annually by 2035 for adaptation, according to UNEP. World leaders called for faster climate action, a just transition away from fossil fuels, greater financial support for vulnerable countries and a stronger focus on implementing existing commitments. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres on November 11 called for unabated coal use to be phased out by 2040 and oil and gas consumption to be cut by a third. Governments, he said, must set credible roadmaps for a just transition away from fossil fuels. Global greenhouse gas emissions must fall by 6 per cent annually, he warned, highlighting that current national climate plans deliver only about a third of the reductions required to keep the 1.5°C temperature goal within reach. Addressing the opening of the Antalya Leaders’ Summit at the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), Guterres said countries must accelerate emissions cuts, protect communities from climate impacts and ensure adequate finance for developing nations.

title: Majority in five of seven countries doubt government readiness for climate change, survey finds
content: Majorities in five of seven countries surveyed believe their governments are unprepared to tackle climate change, according to a new ASRA survey released ahead of COP31. Turkey recorded the highest level of concern, with 72% of respondents saying their government was unprepared, followed by Brazil (69%) and the UK (66%). India was the only country where a majority (51%) expressed confidence in government preparedness, while 45% disagreed. Across all seven countries, most respondents linked climate change to rising food prices, higher household expenses and damage to ecosystems. In India, 72% of respondents associated climate change with forced displacement, while 68% linked it to political conflict or instability. Majorities in five of seven countries surveyed believe their governments are unprepared to tackle climate change, according to a recent survey published by the Accelerator for Systemic Risk Assessment (ASRA). The analysis came ahead of the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP 31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) which began in Antalya, Türkiye on November 9, 2026. The survey, conducted in Australia, Brazil, India, South Africa, Turkey, the United Kingdom and the United States, highlights a gap between public concern about climate change and confidence in governments' ability to respond. Turkey recorded the highest level of concern, with 72 per cent of respondents saying their government was unprepared, followed by Brazil (69 per cent), the UK (66 per cent), South Africa (65 per cent) and the US (62 per cent). Only 15 per cent of respondents in Turkey believed their government was prepared to address climate risks, the lowest level of confidence among the countries surveyed. In Australia, 50 per cent considered their government unprepared, while 34 per cent expressed confidence in its readiness. India was the only country where a majority (51 per cent) believed the government was prepared, compared with 45 per cent who disagreed. The findings were released ahead of the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31), being held in Antalya, Turkey, from November 9 to 20. They follow a September report by the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), Limiting Overshoot , which warned that exceeding the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C warming threshold was widely considered unavoidable under current policies. The findings point to the importance of preparing societies for worsening climate impacts alongside efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Across all seven countries, majorities of respondents believed climate change contributed to rising food prices, ranging from 71 per cent in Australia to 83 per cent in the UK. Between 69 per cent of respondents in Turkey and 82 per cent in Brazil also linked climate change to ecosystem damage and biodiversity loss. At least two-thirds of respondents in every country believed climate change contributed to higher household expenses, including energy and housing costs. The survey also examined public perceptions of climate change's wider social consequences. In Brazil, 81 per cent of respondents believed climate change contributed to forced displacement, while 70 per cent associated it with political conflict or instability. In India, the corresponding figures were 72 per cent and 68 per cent, respectively. Views differed in Australia, where 47 per cent believed climate change contributed a fair amount or a great deal to political conflict or instability, while 44 per cent said it contributed little or not at all.

Bangladesh’s brick kilns found a way to pollute less and earn more, but workers saw no measurable improvement in their pay or working conditions. Simple adjustments to how coal is fed and bricks are stacked helped traditional kilns burn less fuel, release less pollution, and produce better bricks. Yet a companion study found no measurable improvement in wages, health, child labor, or coercive working conditions during the study period. The findings expose a gap between improving an industry’s performance and improving life for its workforce. They also suggest that protecting workers requires measures aimed directly at their needs. The multiyear research effort involved Nina Brooks, an assistant professor at the University of Michigan’s School for Environment and Sustainability and a faculty affiliate of its Center for South Asian Studies. Bangladesh’s rapid urban growth depends on an industry with a substantial environmental footprint. The country is the world’s fourth-largest brick producer, and roughly 8,000 traditional kilns supply more than 90% of its domestic brick consumption. Alongside carbon emissions, the kilns release fine particles known as PM2.5. Ambient air pollution causes 4.9 million premature deaths globally, with South Asia accounting for 32% of them. Brooks began investigating brickmaking about eight years ago during her doctoral studies. She and her collaborators mapped kilns with satellite imagery and machine learning, studied regulation, and examined health effects in communities downwind. Their work revealed why restricting kiln locations alone could not solve the pollution problem. “Bangladesh is one of the world’s most densely populated countries,” Brooks said. “It is not feasible to move brick kilns away from all schools, health facilities, and urban centers that may be harmed by the pollution.” Instead, researchers worked with owners, managers, and workers to improve existing operations. They introduced more continuous coal feeding, brick-stacking arrangements that improved airflow, and measures to reduce heat loss. None required replacing kilns or purchasing major new equipment. After a small pilot, the team expanded the approach to hundreds of kilns. Results published in Science showed that training and technical support reduced energy use by about 10.5% across kilns assigned to the program. Estimated emissions fell by 171 metric tons (about 188.5 US tons) of carbon dioxide and 0.45 metric tons (about 990 pounds) of PM2.5 per kiln over a firing season. Among kilns that adopted the practices because of the program, energy use dropped about 23%, while carbon dioxide and PM2.5 emissions each fell roughly 20%. Owners spent less on fuel and produced a greater proportion of higher-quality bricks. Adoption had increased when researchers returned the next firing season, suggesting the changes had staying power. “Because the changes are economically beneficial for owners, they had a strong incentive to continue following them,” Brooks said. For businesses facing expensive equipment upgrades and authorities struggling to enforce environmental rules, the findings offered a practical route to cleaner production. The researchers then examined whether those business benefits reached workers. Bangladesh’s brick industry relies on a large, mostly informal workforce whose employment can involve debt, advance payments, long hours, hazardous conditions, and restrictions on leaving. A companion study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences examined 246 kilns in the Khulna Division and included private interviews with 1,442 workers. Seventy percent of workers reported having no personal protective equipment, and 71% lacked a formal labor contract. Forty-two percent described restrictions on movement or communication. Across the sample, roughly 20% met the U.S. Department of State’s definitions of labor trafficking. At nearly half the kilns, at least 1 in 6 workers met those definitions. Adult workers also reported child labor at more than 70% of the kilns, with most reported cases involving children ages 14 to 17. The intervention lowered fuel costs by 9.6% and improved brick quality by 8.1%, but researchers detected no corresponding improvement in trafficking, child labor, wages, health, or working conditions. Although changes were possible within the study period, the economic gains did not produce measurable benefits for workers. Higher productivity is often expected to help employees through better pay or conditions. The kiln studies show why that outcome cannot be assumed when coercion and limited bargaining power shape the labor market. “In many countries, not just Bangladesh, labor laws are hard to enforce, particularly in informal sectors. So, it’s critical to find other ways to protect workers from exploitation,” said Grant Miller, a professor of medicine at Stanford University. “Our study shows that we cannot rely on productivity gains alone to do that, at least not in the short run. Finding approaches that work beyond regulation is a central goal of our ongoing research.” Expanding the cleaner production program revealed that kiln owners in other regions were more reluctant to adopt the changes. In districts around Dhaka, owners were considerably less likely to adopt the practices than those in Khulna. Yet participating kilns achieved comparable reductions in fuel use and emissions, Brooks said. “So, we’re seeing greater hesitation,” she said. “But once they adopt, we see the same benefits.” Sameer Maithel, the research team’s lead technical expert, said the reasons are still being investigated. Owners operating on narrow margins may hesitate to change familiar methods while facing unpredictable coal prices, brick demand, and regulation. Differences in kiln size, land, and production practices can also make adoption easier in one location than another. “Informal brick production in South Asia faces a lot of uncertainty: weather, energy prices, market demand, and regulation all shift unpredictably. Many kiln owners also have limited technical and managerial support, and conditions vary from region to region,” Maithel said. “All of this makes scaling up slow and complex, and it takes sustained, dedicated effort.” The lack of improvement for workers has prompted the team to test more direct measures. During the most recent brickmaking season, researchers returned to Khulna with recommendations developed through pilot work and conversations with workers. They recommended masks for people crushing coal, goggles and protective footwear for fire workers, and head protection for brick carriers. Other measures included sanitation and cooking facilities, shaded rest areas, clean water, heat-stress awareness, and information about child labor. “None of the owners I interviewed objected to improving conditions for workers, though some disagreed with specific components. They saw the cost as negligible compared to what they spend running a kiln. As they put it, if workers do better work because of it, it’s worth doing,” said Mohammad Saeed Munim, a research officer in the Health Systems and Population Studies Division of the International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research in Bangladesh. Researchers had expected more resistance. Owners’ willingness to consider these changes now gives the team an opportunity to test whether targeting workers’ daily needs can deliver improvements that greater productivity alone did not. References: “Reducing emissions and air pollution from informal brick kilns: Evidence from Bangladesh” by Nina Brooks, Debashish Biswas, Sameer Maithel, Grant Miller, Aprajit Mahajan, M. Ocean measurements show a vast Southern Hemisphere water layer growing saltier and denser, a shift that could send more heat into deep waters than climate models predict. Every Antarctic summer, melting sea ice sends a vast pulse of fresh water into the ocean. That seasonal supply helps sustain Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW), a layer of relatively fresh seawater that spreads across much of the Southern Hemisphere’s ocean. The AAIW helps store carbon, supply oxygen, and drive global currents, redistributing heat, fresh water, and carbon around the planet. From 1995 to 2015, summer ice melt helped maintain this layer. But from 2016 to 2024, reduced freshwater input left it saltier, denser, and deeper, abruptly reversing its long-term trends in salinity, or salt content, and density. The findings, published in Nature Climate Change , provide the first direct observational evidence of this change in the AAIW’s properties. The international research team analyzed data from the global Argo program, a network of around 4,000 robotic floats that sample the upper oceans, alongside satellite and atmospheric datasets. The study was led by Associate Professor Bishakhdatta Gayen, of the University of Melbourne and the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), and Kaushik Mishra, a PhD student at IISc. Gayen said: “The Antarctic region is the freshwater engine of oceans around the globe. Melting Antarctic sea ice influences circulation thousands of kilometers away. Until 2016, the seasonal summer melt was triple the Amazon River’s entire annual flow of roughly 6,600 cubic km. “From 2016, Antarctic sea ice shrank to record lows. This abruptly choked off that critical seasonal surge, and the meltwater delivery dropped to roughly double the Amazon’s annual flow.” Co-author Professor Alberto Naveira Garabato, of the University of Southampton in the United Kingdom, described the changes as an urgent reminder that climate change is affecting almost every part of Earth’s surface. “As this altered, saltier and denser water mass travels north, it moves across the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans. Because this water layer forms part of the upper limb of the ocean’s global ‘overturning circulation’, a sustained shift could, over years to decades, feed into the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation – the deep-ocean current system often linked to climate stability in the North Atlantic. “It could also ultimately influence atmospheric circulation, weather, and storm tracks in the Southern Hemisphere. However, the impact can cascade globally.” The globe shows sea ice around Antarctica month by month. The first time-series graph shows whether sea-ice area was above or below normal (the 1993-2024 mean), based on satellite observations. The bottom graph tracks the saltiness of Antarctic Intermediate Water, a layer that sinks from the surface into the ocean’s interior, using Argo float data from 2004. From 1993 to 2015, Antarctic sea ice slowly expanded (blue trend line), releasing more freshwater, making the waters beneath it fresher. After 2016, sea ice dropped sharply (red trend line), and the layer turned saltier. Less melting ice means less freshwater reaching the ocean interior. Credit: Kaushik Mishra Changes in how water moves between the surface and deeper layers could also affect the oceans’ role as a “climate buffer,” as Gayen described it. Oceans absorb and redistribute most of the excess heat and a large share of human CO₂ emissions, storing them for decades to centuries. This slows and moderates atmospheric warming and its immediate effects. Mishra said the abrupt reversal revealed a critical missing feedback loop. “The ocean absorbs over 90 percent of all heat released into the environment by human activities, with most of that heat stored in the upper ocean. A weakened AAIW layer could push more excess heat deeper. That would mean existing models are underestimating deep-ocean warming and therefore miscalculating regional sea level rise and long-term ocean and land surface temperatures.” “If the altered AAIW changes the way surface water is carried down into deeper layers, it could affect how much carbon the ocean locks away – although the magnitude and timing are uncertain,” Gayen said. “This could be the tipping point for the Atlantic Ocean and the AAIW current, leading to larger, longer-lasting changes to the climate in the Southern Hemisphere.” According to Gayen, the last time the AAIW switched was at the end of the last interglacial period, around 130,000 years ago, when there was very little ice in Antarctica. “That transition took thousands of years, not two decades,” he said. Reference: “Reversal of Antarctic Intermediate Water trends triggered by sea ice decline” by Kaushik Mishra, Bishakhdatta Gayen and Alberto C. Naveira Garabato, 28 October 2026, Nature Climate Change . DOI: 10.1038/s41558-026-02758-y K.M. acknowledges the Prime Minister’s Research Fellowship (grant no. PMRF-0201843). An El Niño that could beat 1997’s record is taking shape in the Pacific, leaving scientists watching for its next move. El Niño is part of a natural climate pattern that returns roughly every two to seven years. Its most recent very strong events, in 1997–98 and 2015–16, disrupted weather worldwide. Consequences included fires in Indonesia and the Amazon, crop failures caused by drought in southern Africa , and heavy rain and coastal flooding in Southern California. Satellite measurements show that the current El Niño resembles the 1997–98 event, with warm water stretching across the equatorial Pacific to South America. But that oceanic resemblance does not guarantee the same weather during winter 2026–27, as the outcome also depends on how the atmosphere responds. Every El Niño starts with a change in the tropical Pacific’s winds. Trade winds normally push warm surface water westward, leaving sea levels higher in the western Pacific than in the east. When those winds weaken, warm water begins moving back toward the central and eastern Pacific. As warmth spreads eastward, the trade winds weaken further and sometimes reverse, allowing still more warm water to follow. This feedback loop helps El Niño intensify. But strength alone does not determine its effects. The location of the warmest water and the atmosphere’s response also shape the outcome. “The search for the ‘typical’ El Niño is very elusive,” said Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). “They’re all different in terms of where they land and how their impacts play out.” Scientists can track that developing pattern from space because warming water expands, raising the sea surface. Across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, unusually high water therefore provides a signal of El Niño’s heat buildup. The maps compare sea surface height anomalies on October 13, 1997 (left), and October 12, 2026 (right). JPL scientists processed measurements from TOPEX/Poseidon and Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich , respectively. Red shows higher-than-average sea levels, white indicates normal conditions, and blue marks lower levels. Seasonal effects and long-term trends have been removed to highlight El Niño and other short-term natural changes. “What’s unique about altimetry is that we have a 35-year record from nearly identical satellites flying almost the same ground track, with each mission overlapping the next,” Willis said. “That lets us look back in time and compare this El Niño to what happened in 1997. And right now, this one is on track to be even bigger.” Although the 2026 El Niño developed much more abruptly, by October it shared two defining features with 1997: lower sea levels in the west and higher levels in the east, with warm, elevated water reaching South America. Willis thinks that resemblance could translate into similar impacts, including the abundant rainfall seen across California and the southern United States in 1997–98. The powerful 2015–16 event shows why the arrangement of that heat matters. A map based on Jason-2 measurements from October 12, 2015, appears alongside the 1997 and 2026 comparisons. In 2015, the exceptionally warm, high water along the equator did not reach as far against South America. That winter, rainfall effects were concentrated more over Central America and the southeastern United States, with significant flooding in Mexico. NOAA’s October 8, 2026, El Niño outlook assigned an 83 percent chance of a strong to very strong event through the first three months of 2027. Still, its effects during winter 2026–27 and beyond remain uncertain. El Niño’s influence passes through a chaotic atmosphere, and its signal becomes harder to distinguish beyond the tropics. “There’s always a bit of a dice roll here,” Willis said. “Just because this El Niño looks like 1997 doesn’t mean it will be exactly the same—it’s just our best guess at the moment.” Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter.
